module_title: Current Electricity and Ohm's Law (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This level establishes a deep understanding of the microscopic and macroscopic nature of electric current. It covers the drift of charges, the rigorous derivation of Ohm's law, and the physical factors affecting resistance, forming the conceptual bedrock for NEET and JEE Main.

core_concepts.title: Electric Current and Current Density
core_concepts.description: Electric current is the time rate of flow of charge through a cross-section. Instantaneous current is $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$. Although current has a direction (the flow of positive charge), it is a scalar quantity because it does not obey vector addition laws. Conversely, Current Density ($\vec{J}$) is a vector quantity defined as the current flowing per unit cross-sectional area: $J = \frac{I}{A}$ or $I = \int \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{A}$.

core_concepts.title: Drift Velocity ($v_d$)
core_concepts.description: The average unidirectional velocity acquired by free electrons in a conductor under the influence of an external electric field. $v_d = \frac{eE}{m} \tau$, where $\tau$ is the relaxation time. This velocity is extremely small (approx $\approx 10^{-4} \text{ m/s}$). The relation between current and drift velocity is $I = neAv_d$, where $n$ is the number density of free electrons.

core_concepts.title: Mobility ($\mu$)
core_concepts.description: Defined as the magnitude of drift velocity acquired per unit electric field: $\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$. It is always a positive quantity. As temperature increases, the relaxation time ($\tau$) decreases, which consequently causes the mobility of the charge carriers to decrease.

core_concepts.title: Ohm's Law and Its Limitations
core_concepts.description: Under constant physical conditions (like temperature and mechanical strain), the potential difference across a conductor is directly proportional to the current flowing through it: $V = IR$. In microscopic form, this is expressed as $\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{E}$. Limitations: Ohm's law is not a universal law of nature. Devices like diodes, transistors, and liquid electrolytes are non-ohmic; their $V-I$ graphs are non-linear or depend on the sign of $V$.

core_concepts.title: Resistivity and Temperature Dependence
core_concepts.description: Resistance is given by $R = \rho \frac{L}{A}$. Resistivity $\rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$ depends exclusively on the nature of the material and its temperature, not on its dimensions. For metals: As temperature rises, $\tau$ decreases due to more frequent collisions, causing $\rho$ to increase ($\rho_t = \rho_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$). For semiconductors: As temperature rises, the number density $n$ increases exponentially, causing $\rho$ to decrease ($\alpha$ is negative).

core_concepts.title: Electrical Energy and Power
core_concepts.description: The rate at which electrical energy is dissipated in a circuit is Power: $P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$. In a series combination, a lower wattage bulb glows brighter (since $P \propto R$ when $I$ is constant). In a parallel combination, a higher wattage bulb glows brighter (since $P \propto 1/R$ when $V$ is constant).

important_entities.name: Relaxation Time ($\tau$)
important_entities.key_fact: The average time interval between two successive collisions of an electron with the fixed ions.
important_entities.significance: This is the most critical microscopic parameter. When temperature increases, the amplitude of vibration of lattice ions increases, causing collisions to happen more frequently. Thus, $\tau$ decreases, which explains why the resistance of metals increases when heated.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive conceptual error occurs when a wire's length is doubled by stretching, and students assume the resistance merely doubles. When stretched, the volume ($V = AL$) remains strictly constant. Therefore, substituting $A = V/L$ gives $R \propto L^2$. If a wire is stretched to $n$ times its original length, the new resistance becomes $R' = n^2 R$.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: BB ROY of Great Britain had a Very Good Wife (Digits 0 to 9)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: B(Black-0), B(Brown-1), R(Red-2), O(Orange-3), Y(Yellow-4), G(Green-5), B(Blue-6), V(Violet-7), G(Grey-8), W(White-9). For tolerance multipliers: Gold = 5%, Silver = 10%, No Band = 20%.

exam_strategy_tips: NEET frequently features 'percentage change' questions. If the length of a wire is stretched by $x\%$ (where $x < 5\%$), the percentage increase in resistance is directly $2x\%$. This is derived from the error analysis approximation $dR/R = 2 dL/L$.
